title: Not as others without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18)
last: A THREAD THAT RUNS THROUGH THE WHOLE DAY.

cards: The new church in Thessalonica had a fear nobody had prepared them for. They were expecting Jesus to come back soon, maybe within their lifetimes. And then some of their own people died.
A father. A friend. Had those who died missed it?
Were they simply gone? You can hear those questions behind Paul's answer, written for people standing at a grave. It can still be read at a Catholic funeral.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "And we will not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that are asleep, that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope." Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say don't grieve.
He says don't grieve as those without hope. Grief stays. It's the hope that changes it.
And notice the word he uses: asleep.
It's a gentle word for the dead, and a hopeful one: in Paul's picture, sleep is something you wake from.
Then Paul gives the reason for the hope: if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have slept. The dead in Christ won't miss anything.
In Paul's picture, they rise first, and the living meet them, and then: "so shall we be always with the Lord."
And then the practical instruction: "Wherefore, comfort ye one another with these words." This passage isn't a timetable. It's comfort, meant to be said out loud to someone who's grieving.
Catholics put it into practice in many ways. At a funeral, the coffin may be covered with a white pall, recalling the white garment of baptism, and the Easter candle stands beside it.
In November the Church prays for the dead, especially on All Souls' Day. And the Latin preface for funerals says it in four words: vita mutatur, non tollitur.

teach.h: NOT SORROWFUL, EVEN AS OTHERS WHO HAVE NO HOPE.
teach.b: Life is changed, not taken away. Christians grieve. They cry at gravesides like anyone.
For Paul, the grave is not the end of the story.

how: Catholics pray for the dead, especially in November and on All Souls' Day (November 2), have Masses offered for them, and 1 Thessalonians 4 is among the readings for Catholic funerals.

games.q: your friends in Thessalonica are afraid their dead have missed Christ's return. you're Paul. what do you write?
o: tell them grief shows weak faith.
say the dead in Christ will rise, and comfort one another with these words.
say nobody can know anything about it.
games.why: "that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope": the dead in Christ rise, and "so shall we be always with the Lord."

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost; if that's too fresh or too heavy today, choose someone further back, or simply someone the world has lost.
Picture their face, let yourself miss them, then remember one good thing about them that you still carry.
If you pray, pray for them by name, as Catholics do for their dead; if not, simply hold them, and say their name once, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Koimaomai, to fall asleep. Paul's word for the Thessalonian dead: asleep, since sleep is something you wake from. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to fall asleep; Paul's word for the dead in 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

carryVoice: Your line: grieve with hope. Grief stays, and the hope changes it. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.
